utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brdjanin is here. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, welcome. Appearances -- Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours. And can I assure you your robes don't give me a headache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's a tough act at that follow. He's John Ackerman, I'm David Cunningham. We're assisted by Aleksandar Vujic for the Defence. And I have a preliminary matter at the Court's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it has nothing to do with this witness and I have no problem with this witness remaining in the courtroom during this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we are not in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session. I have just welcomed the witness for the third time hoping that the re-examination will be concluded in half an hour. But take your time, Mr. Nicholls. I'm not pushing you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Brown. I'll try to keep my promise and finish in about 30, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I want to do is just go back to some questions that you were asked about paragraph 1.112 of your report, that's on page 39. This is quite a simple matter, but I want to clear it up because you were sort of attacked on this point. In paragraph 112, again talking about cooperation between the military and civilian bodies, you stated: "In a similar manner to the municipal level, cooperative links were also established with the regional government bodies including the Autonomous Region of Krajina (ARK) Crisis Staff, the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly, and other regional government bodies." The next sentence states: "On the 14th of April 1992, a reference in a corps report noted that," and then there is a quote in a document about 5th Corps contacts and meeting with the SAO Serbian autonomous district of Krajina commander. Were you trying to create a misleading impression in any way in the way you wrote this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was trying to use this as an example of the 5th Corps had been involved in establishing cooperative links with regional government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you first list the ARK Crisis Staff, the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly, and then state "and other bodies" and then list this one, this is one of those other bodies you were talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Continuing to the next paragraph, P113, specifically relating to footnote 178, it was suggested that it was misleading to not have submitted this document in support of your -- as you rely on it in support for your contention in footnote 178. I'd like you to be given DB269, please. You can have my copy if it speeds things up. Now, if you look at DB269 and the footnote 178 in its entirety relating to the permit granted to Mr. Brdjanin, do you think that you've included all of the substance necessary to convey what is actually contained in this one-paragraph document, DB269?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it does contain the substance of the document. It isn't a particularly long document, and I think I've included that in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, continuing just on this topic of the permit, there was some discussion about whether or not this was an official duty not appearing on the face of the document to be so necessarily, and whether it supported your contention that tasks were assisted by the 5th Corps, rather than "task." Regarding this permit in DB269 and in your footnote, this is the 26th of June 1992 that the permit is issued. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The ARK -- do you know if the ARK Crisis Staff was in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a permit, is it not, to travel in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As I indicated, I think it comes two days after the initiation of Operation Corridor in the area that's -- that is indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just in general, these types of permits would be -- would need to be issued, would they not, for politicians or anybody to travel in areas of active combat?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in another document we've looked at, we don't necessarily need to look at it again, it's P1598.1, the transcript of the videotape where Mr. Brdjanin is seen being interviewed in Kotor Varos. He stated that it was his responsibility to tour all the front lines and that he most frequently toured the corridor, that he did this because on each Monday, he had to brief or inform presidents of all the Crisis Staffs about the situation. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And for the record, you actually explain and talk about that document in the next paragraph, 1.114.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reference it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. Usher, could you perhaps move -- that's the first one because I think it's obstructing the view of members of the public. That's number one. And secondly, the rest is obstructing my view of Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Brdjanin. So what I suggest you do is you put one -- you move that stack further to the left and put this one in front of it. That's enough. That's enough. You move that in front of it, and then -- not -- at a 90-degree angle. This side. That's enough, yeah. And you move this -- that's enough. You move this further -- nearer to -- no, the interpreters can see. I think -- I can see them well. He can't see the witness. Okay. Just move it somewhere where it doesn't interfere with anyone's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: There is no such a place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Just move it perpendicular with the other one. Just flush with the other one. All right. And move this. If you move it here, it should be okay. That's enough. That's enough. At least this way I can see everyone. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can just try to put this together. If Mr. Brdjanin, as he said, is routinely travelling to combat zones in the corridor and in other areas in order to brief Crisis Staff members, presidents, of what's going on, does it seem logical to you that although we've only got this one permit in evidence that other such permits would have been issued to visit other areas of combat?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. I mean, the Prosecutor at least knows that their obligation here is to prove something beyond a reasonable doubt and, maybe, could have, should have there was another permit sometime somewhere doesn't prove anything. It's pure and complete and total speculation, and this calls for speculation. It's for him to speculate on whether maybe somebody might have issued another permit and maybe a permit was required for somebody who they contend was the highest civilian authority in the region to travel. I mean, it all sounds silly to me. And I think it's just improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was whether -- a suggestion is being made to the witness, and he's being asked whether that suggestion sounds or seems logical to him as a military expert or a military analyst, and that is perfectly legitimate. Go ahead -- or rather, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem logical that other passes were to be disseminated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would expect other similar permits to be issued in similar conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another question on this same point made to you by Mr. Ackerman was who, other than his client, toured areas of combat activity. Because in your report, you state "members of the ARK Crisis Staff," and there was a lot of cross-examination on whether words had an "s" on the end or not. If we look at P1598.1, and I think we probably need to look at it now, you could find on the first page there is a speaker who speaks after Radoslav Brdjanin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who is that next speaker? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin who was head of the Banja Luka security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether he was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So then following on on the next page, you can see that the reporter, Predrag Laketa characterises this visit as a surprise visit to Serbian soldiers by the Krajina leadership. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that. I'd like you to be shown P1583. Very simply, this is the 9th of June 1992 communication from Ratko Mladic concerning the issue of the dismissal of non-Serb officers. We talked about this document in your direct and on cross, but I don't think you actually looked at it on direct or cross-examination. So I just want to confirm this is the Mladic communication which you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, this is cited in footnote 223 of your report covering that topic. I am now going to talk about another topic which you were cross-examined on at some length. It's sort of a mix of topics, the involvement of the army in the confiscation of weapons or operations to remove weapons; in other words, in conjunction with the MUP or the police. And also the ability of local bodies, Crisis Staffs or civilian bodies other than the top leadership to issue orders to military forces. And I'd like you to look at P2419, please. This is a document you footnote that we've referred to before. It's the analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the Army of VRS in 1992. It's in footnote 779. This is a big document. I'm going to direct you to page 158 of the English version which has the heading "basic characteristics of the operational tactical utilisation of the Army of the Republika Srpska." I can give you my copy if that's quicker. It has got English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have an inquiry. The Prosecutor made reference to footnote 779 in his question. And I'm wondering if he's referring to 779 in the report of the witness, which seems to have nothing to do with this document. It might be an error. So for the transcript, maybe we can clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can just look at that first paragraph which talks about how in 1992, the Army of the RS evolved and grew into, as it states, the highest strategical organisational formation of the Serbian people. Can you just tell us looking at that what that tells you about the evolution of the command and control structure of the VRS in 1992.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a section that is repeated a number of times in this document, but I think it indicates that the army grew out of -- or grew under the, as they say themselves, with significant influence and cooperation with the SDS, the Serb organs of government, the orthodox church, and the likes. Earlier on in this document, they go into a little more detail about the actual development of the VRS Main Staff in particular, and the army, and they say that the army can be divided into two phases, the first phase, they're slightly ambiguous with the date. There's one date they say, late May, the other one they say, mid-June, which is up to the first phase. And then the second phase whereby the army was fully established and was able to achieve the strategic goals set it. And in that first phase, a number of times in this document they make reference about the influence, coordination, the importance of the SDS, governmental bodies in the -- not only in the creation of the army, but in the taking control of territory. And in that first phase, they say that -- and they also mention Crisis Staffs I believe in one of the sections, and I can draw your attention to that. In that first phase, they were able to seize control of territories but stop at that, and it was only in the second phase where they were able to expand into the carrying out the strategic objectives such as the corridor, which I think they reference in this document. And I think I can draw your attention to a couple of references, and I think I've also included them in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a document that is being contested by the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me -- that document is in. Let me move on and ask you now some questions about some more -- is there a section you'd like to point us to now?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I have the document. I used it a lot. It is a key document, I believe, and I have referenced in t in my report a number of occasions, and I believe I mentioned it on direct, too. If there's a requirement, maybe, to look at the sections that talk about cooperation or the sections that make reference to Crisis Staff or government bodies and the influence that they had in taking control of territory in that first phase, I can direct the Court to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's in, and I think we covered that pretty well in direct, so we can move on now. For the record, this exhibit appears - we were in error - in footnote 770, 780, 784, and probably some others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I just thought the record should be clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you were right. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to finish, I would just add that this document contains a large number of references to the issue of cooperation, which I know is an issue that has been discussed in the last couple of days. There's a large number of references in that report about the importance placed on cooperation, coordination, as well as those references about that first period whereby government, Crisis Staffs and governmental bodies, I believe they mention regional units and the likes, took control of territory designated as Serb but stopped at that, and then the army itself was able to carry on and achieve the strategic objectives that were set, which I believe is referenced in this quote, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, talking now about the issue of disarmament, I'd like to go through some documents which talk about how that process was, in fact, carried out. If you could be shown P637, please, I first want to talk about Sanski Most. Mr. Ackerman made the point a couple of times during his cross-examination that anybody can issue an order, but it doesn't mean anything unless there was some effect, unless the order is carried out. I'd like to look at some documents pertaining to that issue. I think Mr. Ackerman may have shown you this document yesterday, P637. It's the Crisis Staff decision of 22nd of May 1992. Paragraph 4 talking about disarming formations in Sanski Most -- military -- paramilitary formations in Sanski Most. As far as that is concerned, Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic are charged with putting this into practice. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you know who Colonel Anicic was?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Anicic was the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd now like you to look at P638. This is a document which we looked at during your direct examination. It is an order approved by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Colonel Anicic. We have been through this before a number of times in this case. It's not dated, but on the bottom of -- towards -- on the bottom of page of the English, it talks about an attack beginning on the 26th of May, so that gives us an idea of when this document was written. I just want to draw your attention to paragraph 3, that states: "The 6th Brigade in coordinated action with the STO, Serbian TO units, is undertaking combat operations in Sanski Most Municipality area in order to disarm enemy forces." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that appears to be following the Crisis Staff order, does it not?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and from other documents, in the days following on from this one, operations were conducted in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we know that specifically as referenced in this order, there was a fierce attack on Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to now look at P646, please. This is a 29th of May 1KK report to the Main Staff. It looks like it's signed by General Talic, not for him. I'd like to direct your attention to the first paragraph about halfway through it. The report states as of 29th May: "There is still some weak resistance to confiscation of weapons in the wider area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc." And then it continues. Is that what you were referring to yesterday, not this particular document, but those operations when you talked about the disarmament operations in this area during that time period?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the operations, the reference here to Sanski Most, I talked at some length in the Stakic case about the chain that flowed in relation to disarmament and operations that were conducted there. Later on in this document, in paragraph 2, they talk about cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior and mopping up terrain and confiscating weapons in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. I know the 6th Brigade was involved in Sanski Most. Elements of the 30th partisan division were involved in operations in Kljuc, and elements of the 43rd Brigade and others were involved in operations in Prijedor. But these were all around this time. And as I say in my report, many were couched as disarmament operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you talk about Prijedor in depth in your Stakic testimony which has been admitted, so we won't go into that. However, if you look at this line which you've already identified: "Cooperation with the SRBH MUP in mopping up the terrain and confiscating weapons from illegal formations in these areas," General Talic's assessment with what the 1KK is doing in cooperation with the MUP is almost exactly as written in your paragraph on this point, 2.18, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph again, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 2.18 on page 66.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would argue that is what I've written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, and we're nearly done with Sanski Most, if I could show you P680, this is in your report under footnote 452. There are several interesting parts of this report dated 15th of June 1992 from the security services station in Sanski Most. But this report concerns disarming of so-called paramilitary formations in Sanski Most. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's its title, and it does deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the first paragraph states: "Serbian army units and commands, 6th Brigades, TO, Territorial Defence units, and the SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most municipal area." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we skip down one paragraph to the 25th of May, the document in quotes refers to the military action against Mahala as a "disarming" action. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you would agree that this document also supports, one, that there was cooperation in the confiscation of weapons; and two, that Crisis Staff decisions to confiscate weapons were, in fact, actioned upon.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that demonstrates quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last document on this topic, for Sanski Most, P650, please. This is a Crisis Staff document dated the 30th of May 1992. We've already seen that the Serbian TO of Sanski Most was involved in the assault on Mahala. Simply, this is another order to the Serbian TO stating that now the Serbian Territorial Defence shall prevent all persons from entering the Mahala area except for authorised organs who were involved in mopping up in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that fits as well, doesn't it, with the role of the Serbian Territorial Defence and what its role was in the disarming and attack on Mahala, it follows?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few documents on a similar situation which occurred in Kljuc, if I could show you P921, please, and at the same time P923. If you look at these two documents issued by the Kljuc Municipality Crisis Staff on the 28th of May 1992, the first is an order setting a deadline for citizens to hand over weapons that day by noon; and the second document is another order extending the deadline to the following day, the 29th of May at 10.00. There we have the weapons surrender deadline being set. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd also argue in this document that it appears to be directed very heavily against a Muslim population. I know that was an issue that was discussed yesterday, whether this disarmament was directed to everybody of all ethnicities, and this document would indicate that it was clearly directed at -- in Kljuc, anyway, at the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, thank you, that's a good point. That was another point in contention. In fact, the documents we've looked at from Sanski Most also suggest that it was the Muslim population that was targeted, don't they, because Mahala was a predominantly Muslim area of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Look at P924, now, please. This is regular combat report to the command of the 30th Infantry Division. And it's headed command of the 1st Infantry Brigade, Sipovo command post, 28th of May 1992. If you look at the second page, it states: "Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims do not surrender their weapons by 27 May 1992 at 1200 hours, battalion will carrying out a mopping up operation." I think you may have looked at this document yesterday. Now, that's a bit strange because the report is dated the 28th of May, and it's talking about the 27th of May. So that may be a typo or an earlier deadline which was extended. But could you give me your view on whether this document again shows the issues we're talking about, the involvement of the military in disarming and the fact that it was Muslims areas disarmed, and that the original orders came from Crisis Staffs? Can you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's somewhat similar to Sanski Most. And what did happen in that area was that particular battalion was involved in combat operations around this period. And that is shown from other documentation. I believe it's also referenced in corps level material, too. I think I've referenced a couple of other -- this is a brigade-level combat report, and I think I've referenced one or two other ones in that same brigade in the following days which indicate that that unit was, in fact, involved in the operation as highlighted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we look at P654, I think we can look at one of those corps-level documents you were just talking about. A 1KK command regular combat report of 1st of June 1992 to the Main Staff. Now, if you look at paragraph 3, situation on the ground, the report states: "The areas of Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most are under the control of our units." And then it continues to talk about -- excuse me, on the next page, in paragraph 8, conclusions and anticipated developments. "The mopping up of the town of Prijedor and the neighbouring populated areas is continuing. Mopping up in suburban areas and the seizing of weapons in Muslim-populated villages is also taking place in the municipalities of Kljuc and Sanski Most." Is this one of those documents you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And again, it's another reference in the corps level documents about disarming operations that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at P380 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I know I've gone over my expected time, but I'm getting towards the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll be having a break in seven minutes' time. So try to conclude by then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if I can quite do it by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I should conclude by then? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just looking at this very quickly, another area you talked about yesterday was the imbalance, if you will, of some of the conflict. And you said that there would be just a much greater force and strength on the VRS side in some of these conflicts, and that the reaction seemed excessive, although there were casualties on the VRS side. That's not very well put, but do you understand what I'm saying there?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at the fourth paragraph of this report, P380, it's a 1KK report of 1st of June 1992. That seems to reflect what you were saying. I think you specifically cited Kljuc as one of your examples, does it not?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's one of the examples that you could draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because we've got the citation to two VRS soldiers killed, four seriously wounded, and another 21 slightly wounded. We've gone over a lot in this trial what the response was in Kljuc. And it states here in the paragraph that about 280 enemy soldiers were captured in the Kljuc area and a number of them killed. And we don't have time to go over what some of the other responses were to the killing of these two Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just add as well that as a more generic comment, that these municipalities -- control was taken from the military perspective very, very swiftly. These were not month-long, year-long operations. In some cases, it was over within a matter of days, if that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we actually saw some of that in Sanski Most, the operations beginning around the 25th or 26th of May 1992, the 1KK report stating that the areas were entirely under their control by the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at P657, please, still in the same time frame, this is a 1KK report of the 2nd of June 1992. We talked about it in the direct examination. I think you referred to it yesterday, but you didn't have the document in front of you. It states that there was a conflict - in paragraph 1 - in the area of Lisnja village. And the last sentence of paragraph 2 states: "Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons" -- excuse me. "While because Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that an example of what you were talking about when Mr. Ackerman questioned you and said, look, if an army is attacked, it has got to take care of the area, it has got to secure it. It has got to get rid of the people who are dangerous. Is this an example of an overreaction?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's quite clearly an overreaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you turn the page and look at paragraph 5, combat morale, second-to-last sentence there, it states that it is necessary to ensure both an urgent introduction of a uniformed system of insignia, and it explains why that's necessary earlier in the paragraph. And to reach a decision on placing all Territorial Defence structures under the exclusive command of the SRBH army and the 1st Krajina Corps. I take it that means that up to that point, there clearly wasn't an exclusive command structure over these TO units?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And going back to the combat analysis readiness report and talking about this phase of two phases, in essence, of the growth of the army, the establishment of the army, they make clear reference to that, that there was Territorial Defence units under the influence and control of the SDS, that operated during that period before the formal establishment of the SRBiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because this is the period before the completion of the restructuring to light brigades has taken effect?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think on the 12th of May, there was an announcement that the Territorial Defence should be integrated as a component of the army and that light brigades should be formed as a result of that. But clearly, it took some time to occur. And I know in Prijedor, for example, the Crisis Staff passed a decision in late May making the Territorial Defence a component of the military or ex-JNA brigade that was in Prijedor. So it did take a bit of time to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I have just two more documents to show you, and about two questions. If you could have P1268 and P1282. These documents refer to something we started talking about yesterday, the order of the Prijedor Crisis Staff to establish - I'm sorry - the Intervention Platoon. And you covered this fairly extensively in your Stakic testimony, so I'll do it very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can put my copy on the ELMO if it's quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's much quicker. Okay. We've got the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The order I'm interested in is on page 51 of the English. It's number -- it says number 48 in the top left-hand corner. The ERN is 00866997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is a 17th of June 1992 Prijedor Crisis Staff order to the public security station in the Prijedor regional command to set up a unified Intervention Platoon of 20 members. And it states how this will be made up of soldiers and police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at P1282 on the second page, this is signed by Simo Drljaca. It's to the Crisis Staff of Prijedor dated the 1st of July 1992, couple weeks later. On the second page, he states that the Prijedor SJB has in fact carried out this order.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just -- we don't have much time at all, but could you briefly just state - I know it's difficult - what the Prijedor regional command was and what the Intervention Platoon was, and that's the last question.

utterances.speaker: Ewan Brown [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prijedor regional command was a military command established with Colonel Arsic at its head. He was also concurrently commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade which was a component of the JNA/VRS under General Talic. And the Intervention Platoon is as stated in these documents, a mix of military, police, and civilian police units that operated in the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask one question on recross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Let's see what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want me to tell the question before I ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the practice we've adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I want to do is ask the witness if he has spoken to anyone in the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Since yesterday regarding the testimony he has given in this case or the testimony he might give in the case this morning. And I mean anyone, has he spoken to anyone in the Office of the Prosecutor about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think there's any reason for that question. There's nothing I've brought out in my re-examination today. There's absolutely no reason for that. There's no foundation for the request. I think it's fairly outrageous, and it's so broad it's meaningless cause it could include saying hello to somebody buying a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I will not allow the question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Let me just say for the record that his testimonies seemed extremely well-prepared, and I'm not talking about a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness was here yesterday, and he also heard the request that Mr. Nicholls made to be permitted to approach him and discuss with him on a couple of matters. And my reaction to that, saying no. If you want to indicate, make reference to any document, come here and do it in open Court. So I have no reason to doubt that my advice or my order has been disregarded by both the Prosecution and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It has not, Your Honour. But in reflection, I've no problem with the witness answering whether anybody's prepped him for today in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to make a statement, Mr. Brown, on what Mr. Ackerman has mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really hope I don't have to. I was not prepped for this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any questions? Do you have any questions. And I don't have any questions either which means that your testimony comes to an end here. I thank you, Mr. Brown, for having been patient with us. And you may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll now have a 20-minute break. I'm trying to save as much time as we can. And with your cooperation, Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner, and the interpreters. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've only one request before Your Honour rises. Mr. Ackerman provided a list, or Mr. Cunningham, of documents, but I don't know whether Your Honours have a document that's called BT -- something we've never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me clear up what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's a reference to Prosecutor's 227. I misread the database. In 227 is the ARK Gazette, I think the first 36 entries, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, may I say one other point before you rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's very quick. I intend to submit as exhibits now all of the documents not -- that were cited in his report that have not already been made exhibits because the suggestion has been made that those are necessary. We were trying to save paper, not pour more and more documents, that's why I only put in the ones I referred to on the direct. They were all provided to Mr. Ackerman. I sent him a letter before the direct examination saying if you're missing any of these documents, we'll replace them. But if the suggestion is being made that the report was misleading because all of the footnotes were not entered into evidence, I'd like to provide them all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the point. I'm not concerned about Mr. Ackerman's concerns, as you see them. I'm more concerned about our concerns because if at any time during this trial a submission is made on the -- some -- one or more parts of this report or any other report which supposedly is grounded on a document which is not in evidence, we have a problem. Let's say that the problem arising after all submissions have been made and the case has practically come to an end except for our deliberations. What do we do? We come back here and say Mr. Nicholls, there is a document that has not been tendered in evidence, we would like to refer to it, could you please tender it in evidence. That's the way it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I see the concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can face the problem. I don't know if we'll face it or not, but we could face it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Most of them are in and I'll admit the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's better. And if you can do it in electronic format or in a CD, I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to ask if after we get through these preliminaries that we're about to do that I can be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that mean you'll not be turning up in the afternoon as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what it means, Your Honour. I'll try to come back in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just wanted to make sure. So go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we pretend that the -- we are starting from here. So good afternoon to you, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to give evidence as a Defence witness in this trial, which has been instituted by the Prosecutor against Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Our rules require that before you do so, you enter a -- make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. To help you make this declaration, the usher is going to hand you the text which you're kindly asked to read out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please, take a chair. As I said, if there are problems with interpretation at any time, let me know. We are going to start now. We will finish in about 20 minutes' time. Then you will have a lunch break. And then we continue, then at 3.00 in the afternoon, and we hope to finish by 4.30, without a break in the afternoon. One hour and a half without a break, instead of up to 5.00 with a break. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Boro Blagojevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In what municipality do you currently reside in?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Remember that I'm going to ask you questions, and I would like for you to answer the questions as precisely and concisely as you can. And try to give facts related only to that question. Don't volunteer information because if myself, the Prosecution, or the Chamber needs additional evidence, they will ask you for it. Do you understand those instructions?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And also make sure that you get close enough to the microphone so that your answers can be heard by everyone, including the interpreters. I don't think you need to lean that close to it, but... And you told us you live in the Municipality of Banja Luka. What is your job? What do you do in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am the secretary of the people's assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I've held this position since April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Since April of 2003 or an earlier time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I would like for you to give the Chamber the benefit of your educational history. First of all, obviously you attended secondary school. Where did you attend secondary school at?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. I attended the secondary administrative school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And after completing your studies at the secondary administrative school, did you go on to university?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I graduated from the school of law in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when did you graduate from the law faculty?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And since your graduation in 1987, have you worked as a lawyer or have you worked in administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon graduation, I applied to be an inspector in Velika Kladusa in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I got the job, and I stayed in that job for 11 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where did you go from there, after the 11 months?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: After that, since my salary was rather low in that position, I applied for the job of a revenue inspector in Bosanski Brod Municipality. I got the job, and I stayed in that job from 1988 to 22nd July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. Briefly tell us what you did, what your responsibilities were as a revenue inspector?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Control of taxpayers and the calculation of tax dues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that on 22 July 1991, you left. When you left, did remain in that municipality, or did you go to a different municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I went to my hometown of Banja Luka. I lived there as a tenant. I did not have an apartment of my own. And I had rather large outlays for accommodation and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Once you got to Banja Luka, did you seek employment?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I looked for a job in Banja Luka, and I was willing to consider even jobs that had nothing to do strictly with my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you have a difficult time finding a job in Banja Luka in July and August and after, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have a difficult time because there were at least 200 unemployed lawyers in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you ultimately find a job in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the revenue administration in Banja Luka, and I asked if they had a vacancy for an inspector. They told me there were no vacancies at the moment, but that there is a vacancy in the commune of municipalities, the joint municipalities, and that vacancy was for an administrator or a director.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ultimately get that job?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I wrote my application to apply for that job. And when in September 1991 they had a session, I was taken on that job, the job of secretary of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The organ concerned is the association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And we're going to come back and discuss in more detail your dealings with the association of municipalities, so I don't need a great deal of detail now. But tell the Chamber how long you remained with the association of municipalities or any other entity that evolved from it. And specifically, I'm talking about ARK.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed in the municipality of the autonomous region as long as it existed. That was on the 14th of September 1991 they ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where did you work after 14 September 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: After that date, I was jobless. The region did not exist any more, and I was out of a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And very briefly, when did you go back to work after losing your job on 14 September 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I returned -- I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure. You told us that you lost your job on 14 September 1991. And I take it there was a period of time that you were jobless. What I'm trying to find out is when you next went back to work and what sort of work you did.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of March 1993, I found employment again in the national assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what position did you initially have with the national assembly with the RS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a deputies' centre or assemblymen's centre, situated in the building of the municipality. It was a room where all delegates from the Bosnian Krajina met. I got a job there. Since the headquarters of the national assembly was at Pale, and I was unable to go there, that's where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what were your job responsibilities at this job?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Occasionally, sessions of the council of the national assembly for the economy and finances were held in Banja Luka. And I would serve there as the secretary of that council, drawing up minutes, doing things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And have you been with the national assembly since the date that you mentioned? I think March -- 1st March 1993.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been there since the 1st of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in your current position, what are your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my current responsibilities include preparing of the sessions of the national assembly and all the background material required for these sessions; preparation of laws for publishing in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions about your party affiliation. Are you now or have you ever been a member of the League of Communists, the communist party?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, I was a member of the League of Communists. Currently, I am not a member of any party because my job is the job of a civil servant. Civil servants may not be affiliated with political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I understand that you're not currently affiliated with a political party. But were you ever affiliated with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I have never been an SDS member. I was for a while, however, a member of the SNS, the party of Mrs. Plavsic when she was the head of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'm at an area where I would like to go into private session based on what he has indicated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while and we'll see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After you left your job in Bosanski Brod and went back to Banja Luka, were you living in Banja Luka when a group known as the SOS appeared in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you working in the municipal building, the municipality building at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what happened to you the day that the SOS appeared in Banja Luka? Were you able to -- for example, were you able to get to work that day?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I set out to go to work that day. But at an intersection I was turned by back a group of people. They told me I could not go on and I had to go back home. I didn't know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This group of people that turned you back and sent you home, how were they dressed? Were they in civilian clothes or other clothes?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were all dressed differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I guess the operative question is did they have guns? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And in your job -- at this point, you're working for the association of municipalities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your role with that association, did you have any dealings with anyone beyond what you just described --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think in the SOS is April 6, 1992. By that stage, the association of the municipalities is the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I appreciate the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At the time the SOS arrives in April 1992, you're working for what entity?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the secretary of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And that day that they appeared in April of 1992, beyond what you've just described, being sent home in effect by a group of people, did you have any other dealings with the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You obviously were not involved in any sort of negotiation, discussions with anyone with the SOS, I take it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to ask he's not to lead on matters like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think Ms. Korner is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you involved in any discussions with any representatives of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In April 1992, did you have any idea who might be the leader of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Nenad Stevandic? Does that name -- is that name familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I had never heard of him except that once when I received the decision on the Crisis Staff. That's when I saw that name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if I could show, with the usher's assistance, show the witness P168. Mr. Witness, that's a document that you've seen before. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That is a document -- 168 is a decision signed by Nikola Erceg setting forth the members of the ARK Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Number 15 is the individual we just mentioned, Mr. Stevandic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how it was that he got selected to serve on the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good breaking point if it's in the Court's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham. I thank you. We'll now have a lunch break, and we will resume at 3.00. You'll be looked after, attended to by our staff. And you can now be -- he can leave the courtroom now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll reconvene at 3.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m. ---On resuming at 3.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, at the break we were talking about events in April and May of 1992. What I want to do now is backtrack, go back in time, to the time that you spent working for the association of municipalities. Do you remember again what month it was that you started working for the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: September of 1992 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was the position that you had with the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I applied for the job of the secretary of the association of municipalities, and that is the job that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 2354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Binder 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What were your job responsibilities as secretary of the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of organising the sessions of the assembly of the association of municipalities. I was supposed to secure the room where the sessions would be taking place, and I was also taking the minutes of all of these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you started there in September of 1991, were there any other employees, paid employees, of the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the association of municipalities you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want you -- you have in front of you Exhibit P2354. I want to make sure that you recognise that document. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw it when I first joined. The association of municipalities in May of that year, that was in 1991, the municipalities that joined in the association signed this document in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. And obviously, the association that we have been talking about for the past several minutes is the association of municipalities for Bosanska Krajina. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the time that you were the secretary, I take it -- or did you have the opportunity to read the statute?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you know based on that reading and any other source what the purpose of this association was? Why was this association formed, is a better way of asking the question, if you know.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the amendments of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the amendment 42 dating from 1997, the municipalities which were connected especially were able to join into an association of municipalities in order to further their economic advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was this association a voluntary association or a mandatory one?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a voluntary association.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether the municipality of Prijedor joined the association?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if you know, could you tell us why they didn't join? And if you don't know, that's okay, too. You can just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they didn't join at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was this association intended to be strictly a Serbian entity? That means for Serbs only?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. This was done based on the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in the time that you were with the association, were there non-Serb members, non-Serb members of the assembly of this association?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were representatives coming from the non-Serb parts of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like for you to open Exhibit 2354, Prosecutor's 2354, find Article 35. And I'd like for you to read Article 35 silently to yourself. And when you're done reading Article 35, let us know.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you read the second paragraph as well?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. Were the decisions of the association of municipalities, specifically the assembly of that association, were they binding on member municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were providing those municipalities ratified them at the sessions of their respective assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If there was no ratification, would there be a legal law? Would there be a legal pronouncement?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Those municipalities did not have to abide by those decisions in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like for you to look at Article 38 which deals -- is under the heading of "amendments." I'd like you to find that portion. It's about four paragraphs long. I'd like you to read it silently to yourself and let us know when you're done reading it because I'm going to ask you some questions about that. Ready? Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Article 38. Yes, that is a proposal to amend the statute of the association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on your understanding of administrations as well as your understanding of the law, does Article 38 set out the only way that the statute can be amended?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Any amendment of the statute can -- could be done following the proposal of the assembly of the association of municipalities, or the executive council of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What would happen -- what effect, if any, would an amendment have if it didn't follow this procedure?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It would be contrary to the statute of the association, that is, of the region. And then it wouldn't be binding upon the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit. And I'd like to show the witness, just so they're available, Prosecutor's 80 and 81, please. You told us that you started working for the association in September of 1991. At around that same time, did the association change its name?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It became the Autonomous Region of Krajina, so it's name was the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what position -- did you continue to work for the ARK?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the secretary of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You had the same -- I take it you had the same position you had when you worked for the association of municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: By this time, had anyone else been hired to join you as an employee of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was just one professional, that was the president of the assembly, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin. He was the only professional, gainfully employed professional. There were just the two of us fully employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When the association of municipalities changed into the ARK, did its competence change, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned Mr. Kupresanin's name as being the other employee. Because of his position and your position, did you develop a professional relationship? By that I mean, did you work with him on a daily or regular basis?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Kupresanin in the course of your duties? How often, say, during a typical workweek would you see him and work with him, talk with him?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, in April of that year, he had a heart failure, so he spent a lot of time in various spas, in rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So tell the Chamber what that means in terms of you -- how often you would see him, how often you would work with him. What was your relationship with him like?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Due to his medical condition, during that period of time, I would see him very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to take you now to April of 1992. Are you still holding the same position with the ARK that you've described for the Chamber? Do you still have that job?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In April, specifically towards the end of April of the year 1992, did you become aware of instructions that were promulgated and signed by Prime Minister Branko Dzeric?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness, please --

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I read about that in the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like with the usher's assistance show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 157 and make sure that you and I are talking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, any time I hand you a document, I want it to be understood that -- I'd like for it to be understood that you can have as much time as you need to examine the document, become acquainted with the document, because I don't want to talk about a document that you haven't had a chance to look at.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We know just by reading the heading of the document it's an excerpt from instructions for the work of the municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people. Was there ever any similar document to this that dealt with, if you will, regional Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Does this document ever mention, to the best of your knowledge, regional Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in this document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you were working for the ARK when this document -- when you found out about this document, when you read it, what effect, if any, did it have on you?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit. And I'd like to talk to the witness now about Prosecutor's Exhibit 167. Let me know when you're ready because I'd like to ask you some questions about this, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This is obviously a document 4 May 1992 attributed to the secretary of the regional secretariat for national defence, Colonel Sajic. I want you to look at under the decision paragraph number 5, does that paragraph deal with disarmament of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated 4 May 1992. In the days after 4 May 1992, did you continue to work for the ARK when it was -- when the ARK Crisis Staff was in existence?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in the days that followed this decision in P167 dated 4 May 1992, did the ARK Crisis Staff issue documents dealing with disarmament of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did it issue any?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did they issue -- was that a topic that was contained in conclusions by the ARK Crisis Staff, the subject of disarmament of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They constantly appealed to paramilitary formations to hand in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. We can see from the face of the document that it was generated by the republic's secretariat of national defence. If you know, when did this republic secretariat for national defence or the regional secretariat for national defence, do you know when that came into existence?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. But I believe that it was on the 4th of March 1992 that the Assembly of the Autonomous Region appointed the Executive Committee which had several secretariats. But I don't know whether the secretariat for national defence was among them. But I'm not sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know when, if at all, the regional secretariat was up and running, to use a word that I've heard you use before, when it was alive?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether it actually started operating because according to a decision of the Crisis Staff passed on the 15th of May, it was appealed that the work of the regional secretariat for national defence should be organised, that is 11 days after this decision that I can see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let's go ahead and put Prosecutor's Exhibit 227 in front of you and go to the conclusions of 15 May 1992, which is entry 11. Again, that's 15 May 1992. And I will direct your attention down to number 4.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I stand corrected if I said anything else. Yeah, it is 15 May. It's the conclusions that day, and I would direct your attention to number 4.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In conclusion number 4, it says: "The operation of the regional secretariat for national defence should be immediately organised." So we can see from this that it hadn't been organised yet at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know, to jump ahead a little bit, do you know whether or not it was ever organised?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you were present at ARK Crisis Staff meetings, and I know that you have read the Gazette, the ARK Gazette, that contains the decisions and conclusions. Would it be safe to say that the subject of disarmament of paramilitaries was a topic of conversation among those who attended the Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I really do think this is quite an important topic, and I think it is right the witness should give his own answers and not be led on what was the topic of conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the subject of paramilitaries ever come up at ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when the subject came up, which ethnicities, if any, were of concern to the people in attendance?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that they discussed any particular ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did they discuss Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that a concern of people in attendance at ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather prefer to have a more clear-cut answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's what I'm going to try to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, because this probably -- I mean, it's...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like for you to give this Chamber an idea of if the topic was discussed, how often it was discussed, meaning did it come up every meeting, once a week, once a month? Give the Chamber an idea of how often this subject came up.

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to recall that now. But very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I would like for you to get even more specific if you can. When you say "very frequently," how often was it? Did it come up at each meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see from the conclusions every time conclusions were adopted, and included a conclusion on that issue, that means that the discussion centered, among other things, on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
